captions: Let's break down the Sham Foam I-P-O — a small,
forty-crore S-M-E issue from a foam and furniture maker in Haryana.
We'll cover what it does, its financials,
where the money goes,
how it stacks up against the big listed name,
and how much you'd need to apply.
This is education, not investment advice.
So what does Sham Foam do?
It manufactures foam-based products and furniture,
from its base in Ambala, Haryana.
One thing to understand about foam: it's made from chemicals whose prices track crude oil.
So the company's raw-material costs —
and therefore its margins — swing with oil prices,
which is a real risk.
And this is a fixed-price S-M-E issue at a hundred and thirty rupees a share —
a small, lightly-covered offering,
so expect thin research and thin trading.
Let's go deeper.
Sham Foam makes mattresses — memory-foam,
hybrid and orthopedic — and P-U foam products,
from Ambala in Haryana, led by its founders,
the Jindal family.
It sells through dealers and direct factory delivery,
backed by long warranties, competing in a branded,
distribution-led mattress market.
On order book —
as a make-to-stock manufacturer it doesn't disclose one.
So judge this one on its revenue trend and margins,
rather than on any forward-order visibility.
Now the financials.
For the year to March twenty twenty-four,
revenue was about eighty-one crore,
with net profit of roughly three point five eight crore.
Notice the margin —
profit is only about four percent of revenue, which is thin.
And the recent numbers look lumpy across reporting periods,
so read the offer document carefully to understand the trend before you form a view.
Where does your money go?
And here Sham Foam has the best possible answer —
this is a hundred percent fresh issue.
There's no offer for sale at all.
Every rupee raised goes into the company,
not into a promoter's pocket.
For a small, growing manufacturer that needs capital,
that's exactly the structure you want to see.
What does the fresh money fund?
Mostly working capital,
which a manufacturing business ties up in raw materials and inventory.
Part supports capacity and equipment so it can make more product,
and the rest is general corporate purposes.
So the money is aimed at running and growing the business —
the right use for a young manufacturer.
Now — the competitors.
The obvious listed name in foam is Sheela Foam,
the company behind Sleepwell.
But it's vastly bigger and branded,
so it's a reference for scale,
not a real peer for a tiny S-M-E like this.
As we said, foam is made from crude-linked chemicals,
so margins move with oil prices,
and furniture is a competitive, commoditised trade.
With no comparable listed company at this size,
there's no meaningful P-E to compare —
so weigh the fixed price of one hundred and thirty rupees against Sham Foam's small and rather uneven profits,
and read the offer document carefully.
Should you subscribe?
The strengths —
it's a hundred percent fresh issue with no promoter cashing out,
and it has a reasonable revenue base of about eighty crore.
The watch-outs — margins are thin at around four percent,
the recent numbers are lumpy, its costs swing with crude oil,
and it's a tiny S-M-E with a big minimum bid and thin trading.
The takeaway — a cleanly-structured micro-cap,
but a thin-margin, input-cost-sensitive one.
Read the offer document closely before you decide.
Now — how to apply, and how S-M-E I-P-Os differ.
Sham Foam lists on the N-S-E S-M-E platform,
separate from the mainboard.
The minimum is large.
One lot is a thousand shares —
about one lakh thirty thousand rupees —
and the smallest retail application is two lots,
roughly two lakh sixty thousand rupees.
That's a big ticket versus a mainboard I-P-O.
And remember, S-M-E stocks are volatile and lightly traded,
so only commit money you can lock away.
Track the live subscription on the N-S-E S-M-E page,
Chittorgarh, or your broker app —
allotment is by lottery if oversubscribed.
Let's recap Sham Foam.
A foam and furniture maker from Ambala,
with a reasonable revenue base but thin, lumpy profits.
The best feature is the structure —
a hundred percent fresh issue, no promoter selling.
But margins are thin and swing with crude,
there's no listed peer to benchmark,
and the S-M-E minimum is about two lakh sixty thousand rupees.
This video explains the IPO for education only —
it is not investment advice,
not a buy or sell recommendation,
and not a prediction of listing gains.
Grey-market premium is unofficial and changes hourly.
Always read the RHP and check the live subscription before you apply.
Thanks for watching.
